content: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 17α-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare form of CAH caused by mutations in the CYP17A1 gene. This gene encodes an enzyme that plays a critical role in the synthesis of cortisol and sex steroids. The enzyme has dual functions, acting as both a 17α-hydroxylase and a 17,20-lyase, mediating key steps in steroidogenesis. Defects in this enzyme result in a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations, depending on the degree of enzymatic impairment. In individuals with 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, the production of cortisol is inefficient, leading to elevated levels of ACTH. However, corticosterone, a weak glucocorticoid, is produced in sufficient quantities to prevent adrenal crisis. The deficiency also impairs sex steroid synthesis, resulting in underdeveloped secondary sexual characteristics. Genetic females (XX) typically present with normal female internal and external anatomy at birth but fail to undergo puberty due to the lack of sex steroid production. They exhibit delayed puberty, with absent breast development and pubic hair, elevated gonadotropins, and an infantile uterus. Imaging confirms the presence of ovaries, but ovulation is often absent even with estrogen replacement. Some milder cases allow for partial breast development and irregular menstruation, but fertility is generally reduced. In genetic males (XY), the deficiency leads to reduced fetal testosterone production, resulting in varying degrees of undervirilization. External genitalia may range from normal female to ambiguous or mildly underdeveloped male. The most common phenotype includes a small phallus, perineal hypospadias, a blind-ending pseudovaginal pouch, and intra-abdominal or inguinal testes. Wolffian duct structures may be hypoplastic or normal, depending on the degree of testosterone deficiency. Some individuals with partial virilization develop gynecomastia at puberty. Hypertension, a hallmark of this condition, distinguishes it from other forms of androgen deficiency or insensitivity. Fertility is impaired in those with significant testosterone deficiency. Mineralocorticoid excess is a prominent feature of 17α-hydroxylase deficiency. The adrenal cortex becomes hyperplastic and overstimulated, leading to elevated levels of deoxycorticosterone (DOC), corticosterone, and 18-deoxycorticosterone. These precursors, though weaker mineralocorticoids, are produced in sufficient quantities to cause volume expansion, hypertension, and hypokalemia. Renin and aldosterone levels are suppressed. Hypertension often develops in infancy or childhood, with nearly 90% of affected individuals exhibiting low-renin hypertension by late childhood. Hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis are common due to urinary potassium wasting. A small subset of individuals has been reported with isolated 17,20-lyase deficiency, which primarily affects sex steroid synthesis without significant impact on mineralocorticoid or glucocorticoid production. These individuals do not develop adrenal hyperplasia, mineralocorticoid overproduction, or hypertension. The clinical presentation is similar to 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, with impaired pubertal development and infertility. Treatment involves glucocorticoid replacement to suppress ACTH, normalize mineralocorticoid production, and lower blood pressure. Genetic females (XX) typically require estrogen replacement to induce puberty and periodic progestin to regulate menstruation. Fertility is often reduced due to poor ovarian steroidogenesis and ovulation. Management of genetic males (XY) with ambiguous genitalia is more complex. Severely undervirilized individuals are often raised as females, with surgical removal of nonfunctional testes. If raised as males, testosterone replacement is necessary to induce puberty and maintain masculinization throughout adulthood. Surgical correction of hypospadias and orchiopexy may be performed if feasible. Hypertension and mineralocorticoid excess are managed with glucocorticoid therapy, as in other forms of CAH. Related chapters on CAH provide further details on management strategies and support resources for affected individuals and families.
